title: On the Incarnation
hookLine: Athanasius, at about twenty-five, explains why the Word became flesh

lines: A KING MOVES INTO ONE HOUSE.
WHY WOULD THE WORD BECOME HUMAN?
cards: A great king enters a great city and moves into one house on one street. Just one. And yet, the story goes, the whole city is honored.
Robbers who had been circling it lose their nerve, because the king lives there now. That small parable comes from a short book by Athanasius, who became bishop of Alexandria.
The book asks a question at the center of the Christian story: why would God's Word become a human being? Its title is today's word: On the Incarnation.

teach.b: Athanasius starts with a problem. People were made in God's image, made from nothing and held in being by God. But turning from God, they were sliding back toward nothing: toward death and decay.
And God, he says, couldn't simply watch his own work fall apart. That would be unworthy of God. Here he gives a second picture.
A portrait painted on wood has been ruined, smeared until the face is gone. The painter doesn't throw away the board.

teach.h: A PORTRAIT REDRAWN ON THE SAME WOOD.
teach.b: The person in the portrait comes back and sits again, so the likeness can be redrawn on the same wood. That, for Athanasius, is the Incarnation.
The Word of God came and took a body like ours, so the image could be restored from inside humanity, and death undone by his rising.
Paul has a line for the coming down: Christ "took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men."
Now the king in the city makes sense. By living in one human body, the Word honored every human body, and the powers that preyed on us lost their grip.
Near the end of the book, Athanasius says it in one breath, here in paraphrase: he became human so that we might be made divine. Orthodox Christians call that sharing theosis.

Catholics and some Protestants speak of it in the words of Second Peter: "partakers of the divine nature." Churches describe it differently. Athanasius's starting point is plain enough: God didn't stay far away.

how: Christians confess in the Nicene Creed that the Son of God was incarnate and made man; churches celebrate the Incarnation at Christmas and the Annunciation.

a creed recited when a new bishop is chosen
Athanasius's book on why God's Word became human

games.q: a king in the city — tap the pairs.

s: Athanasius says God rescued humanity from a distance, by decree
he says the Word took a body like ours and restored God's image from the inside.
in Athanasius's picture, a king lives in one house and the whole city is honored
by living in one human body, the Word honored every human body.
Athanasius compared humanity to a ruined portrait the subject comes back to redraw
the painter keeps the board; the person sits again so the likeness can be restored.

games.q: you're a painter. a portrait on wood has been smeared until the face is gone. what do you do?
o: throw away the board and start over.
have the person sit again and redraw the face on the same wood.
games.why: that's Athanasius's picture of the Incarnation: the Word comes in person, so God's image can be restored in the same humanity, not replaced.

practice: Hold Athanasius's picture, in paraphrase: the person in the portrait comes back and sits again, so the likeness can be redrawn on the same wood.

Think of one thing in your own life that feels smeared or ruined, and let the picture sit beside it without forcing anything: the wood isn't thrown away, it's kept and worked on. If you pray, you can offer it to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: On the Incarnation. Athanasius's short book on why the Word of God became human: to restore God's image in us from the inside, like a king who moves into the city.

orig.note: Greek: becoming human, the word in the title of Athanasius's book, On the Incarnation.
